_what_this_is: The last time anyone checked whether upstream moved. Distinct from upstream-review.json, which records the versions a human has REVIEWED. This file records only that a LOOK happened, and what it saw.
_why_it_exists: Every dependency floats to latest at build time, and the marker test in upstream-review.json fires when a build happens -- but nothing makes a build happen. Releases are manual, so a quiet month is a month in which upstream can move unobserved. The marker catches 'we are about to ship a version nobody reviewed'; this catches 'upstream moved while nobody was looking'.
_why_this_is_enough: A scheduled CI poller was the obvious answer and is not needed here. This project is built entirely through an agent, so a directive in CLAUDE.md runs on every working session by construction -- the check happens because work happens. Dependabot cannot do this job anyway: verified 2026-08-14 against dependabot-core's own test table, a NuGet Version="*" is rewritten to "*" and produces no PR, and npm "latest" is skipped by a dist-tag guard. Dependabot bumps declared floors, and this project declares none.
_how_to_resolve: Resolve each upstream the way the BUILD resolves it, not the way a registry query defaults. In particular playwright-core is NOT npm 'latest' -- it arrives as @playwright/mcp's own exact dependency. On 2026-08-15 npm 'latest' for playwright-core was 1.62.1 while the version that actually ships is 1.63.0-alpha-2026-08-05, because upstream publishes daily alphas and pins one exactly. Checking 'latest' would have reported drift that does not exist, in the safe direction that day and the unsafe direction on 2026-09-14. That is the whole rule and there is no second case. *Corrected 2026-09-21 (previously a paragraph beginning "SINCE 2026-09-17 THE BUILD RESOLVES playwright-core THROUGH AN OVERRIDE, and that is a third way to get this row wrong", which went on to say the version this row records is the override, read from `overrides.playwright-core` in build/payload/package.json, and that THE EXIT CHECK IS THE SAME READ, DONE TWICE).* THE OVERRIDE IS GONE. It was a dated exception taken 2026-09-17 and it ended 2026-09-21 when @playwright/mcp 0.0.82 shipped a playwright-core carrying the fix it was taken for; build/payload/package.json carries no `overrides` block, and the two instruments that read the exit were retired with it. So this row is read out of @playwright/mcp's own dependencies again, and `packages['node_modules/playwright-core'].version` in the lock beside it must AGREE -- that agreement is the invariant now, asserted by PayloadTests.TheLockRecordsUpstreamsOwnExactPinOfPlaywrightCore and by build/Build-Payload.ps1, and a disagreement means something is holding the version somewhere else. ONE THING THE OVERRIDE LEFT BEHIND, and it is about reading rather than resolving: @playwright/mcp 0.0.82 pins 1.64.0-alpha-1789764292000, a 13-digit epoch-milliseconds alpha rather than the `alpha-YYYY-MM-DD` shape upstream publishes daily. Nothing in this tree orders these strings any more -- every comparison is for IDENTITY against another recorded string -- so record what you read and do not try to parse a date out of it.
_honesty_rule: Only stamp lastChecked after a lookup actually returned a version. A date written from intent rather than from a result is worse than no date, because it reads identically to a real one and silences the next check for a day.
result: Checked 2026-09-23, the morning after 1.1.0 was cut and the same day it was published. NO DRIFT ON ANY OF THE FIVE, AND NONE ON THE VENDORED ROW -- the first all-clear since 2026-09-21, and it is what a release day should look like: every version the build resolves is a version somebody has reviewed. @playwright/mcp 0.0.82 (published 2026-09-18T23:38:28.161Z, unmoved across 435 published versions); playwright-core 1.64.0-alpha-1789764292000, read out of 0.0.82's own dependencies object and NOT npm `latest`, which is the trap this row exists for; ModelContextProtocol 2.2.0 across 47 versions; Velopack 1.2.158 across 119 versions, reviewed and adopted yesterday; node v24.21.0 Krypton, released 2026-09-07, still the newest entry carrying an `lts` field. The vendored SQLite amalgamation re-read from the same machine-readable PRODUCT line: 3.53.4, 2,946,650 bytes, SHA3-256 628a44cfe82c66aed1ccbbe85a562d2e33ebe64b3288981ed76285612227934e -- identical to the pin in all three fields. THE POSITIVE CONTROL IS STILL BORROWED FROM OUTSIDE THE FIVE and still discriminates: System.Text.Json lists 181 versions whose newest in any form is 11.0.0-rc.1.26425.128 against a newest stable of 10.0.12. _why_vendored_is_a_separate_section: `resolved` above is the five upstreams the BUILD floats to latest, and UpstreamReviewTests.TheFiveReviewedUpstreamsAreTheOnesTheDriftCheckResolves holds that set identical, in both directions, to upstream-review.json's. `vendored` below is source PINNED inside this tree: it does not float, no build resolves it, it has no golden snapshot to diff, and reviewing it is a human downloading one zip and re-running the gate. Putting it in `resolved` would either break that correspondence or force a name into upstream-review.json that no review procedure applies to -- and editing upstream-review.json to make a test pass is exactly what CLAUDE.md forbids. So a pin is never counted as a float, and the row below carries its own `checked` date because the top-level `lastChecked` is about the five.

sqlite-amalgamation.how: sqlite.org/download.html, and read the MACHINE-READABLE line rather than the rendered table: the page source carries `PRODUCT,<version>,<year>/sqlite-amalgamation-<n>.zip,<bytes>,<sha3-256>` for exactly this artifact. Download that URL, check the SHA3-256 BEFORE unzipping, and take sqlite3.c and sqlite3.h. This is NOT a registry query and NOT an npm or nuget `latest`: no maintained package carries this source at all, which is why it is pinned here. The cross-check is the floating `SourceGear.sqlite3` nuget version, whose version number IS the SQLite version and which lags sqlite.org by 3-30 days -- and since 2026-08-26 it costs nothing to read, because the test project references it (it is what puts an e_sqlite3.dll beside a CoreCLR test host) so every re-resolve writes today's SQLite into tests/BrowserAI.Tests/packages.lock.json. A gap between that number and `pinned` above is a prompt to look, never a defect on its own: the package skips some releases. READ 2026-09-22 AND THE GAP IS ZERO FOR THE FIRST TIME SINCE THIS SENTENCE WAS WRITTEN: SourceGear.sqlite3 resolves 3.53.4 in tests/BrowserAI.Tests/packages.lock.json, the same version sqlite.org's PRODUCT line carries, so the 3-30 day lag the paragraph above describes is nil today and there is nothing to look at. A gap is a prompt; its absence is not evidence of anything either.
sqlite-amalgamation.watch: ericsink/SQLitePCL.raw issue 657, 'Provide static libraries for Native AOT deployment' -- open since 2025-12-27, owner said 2026-01-08 he plans to work on it. The 3.x line already ships libe_sqlite3.a for fourteen Linux RIDs and nothing for win-*. THE DAY a win-x64 e_sqlite3.lib ships inside SourceGear.sqlite3, build/Sqlite.targets' compile step is deleted, <NativeLibrary> points into the restored package, and the native floats again like everything else. Check it by globbing the restored package for a .lib under runtimes/win-x64 -- a glob for *.a in the same package returns twenty, which is the positive control that the glob shape works.
